# Classification Ensembles {#sec-cls-ensembles}


```{r}

#| include: false

```

While classification trees are interesting and flexible models, as we saw in the previous chapter, they often rank poorly in prediction. Two of the reasons are: 

- The granularity of predictions from rectangular trees is often low since the number of unique predicted values is the same as the number of terminal nodes. 
- Their high model variance contributes to an overall high model mean squared error (recalling @sec-variance-bias).  Breiman [1994] labeled tree-based models as being an _unstable procedure_. 

In this chapter, we discuss methods for bundling many classification trees into an overall ensemble model. As we'll see, tree ensembles have a well-earned reputation for exceptionally high accuracy. 

We'll start with ensembles of independently generated trees (bagging and random forests), then move to Bayesian ensembles, and finish with ensembles assembled sequentially (boosting). We'll also discuss two rule-based ensembles.

## Bagging {#sec-cls-bag}


```{r}
#| label: forest-bag-cart
#| include: false
#| cache: true

cart_bag_spec <-
  bag_tree(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("rpart", times = 50)

set.seed(285)
forest_cart_bag_res <-
  cart_bag_spec |>
  fit_resamples(
    class ~ .,
    resamples = forested_rs,
    control = control_resamples(
      save_pred = TRUE,
      save_workflow = TRUE
    ),
    metrics = cls_mtr
  )

forest_cart_bag_best <- select_best(forest_cart_bag_res, metric = "brier_class")

forest_cart_bag_pred <-
  forest_cart_bag_res |>
  collect_predictions(parameters = forest_cart_bag_best) |>
  mutate(wflow_id = "Bagged CART") |>
  relocate(wflow_id)

forest_cart_bag_mtr_ex <-
  forest_cart_bag_pred |>
  cls_mtr(class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes)
```


Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregation, was first popularized by @breiman1996. The most commonly used definition of a bagged tree is a collection of decision trees grown to maximum size (i.e., unpruned with a small $n_{min}$) and trained on a bootstrap sample of the training set. If we create an ensemble of $T$ trees, we obtain a collection of $T$ predictions for each data point. The final prediction summarizes the collection. Most often the proportion of hard-class "votes" from each tree is used for probability estimates, although other estimators, such as the mean of the class probabilities, can also be used. 

Using many trees solves the two issues mentioned above. The ensemble's overall model variance is much smaller than a single tree's. STANDARD ERROR OF BETA MEAN?. Since trees are very flexible, they have low model bias. Combined with lower ensemble variance, this makes the overall model error very low and therefore more predictive. 

Practically, combining $T$ predictions means the predicted values are more granular. To achieve stable performance, $25 \le T \le 50$ is often a good range. However, this is not a tuning parameter; we just need enough ensemble members to obtain a good mean estimate. 

The key thing to realize about bagging is that it only improves high-variance models. Consider logistic regression, where the model estimates parameters using all training data points. Adding or removing rows from the training set, or jittering their values, has a relatively limited effect on predictions. This model has low variance, so averaging its predictions has little impact; we are averaging very similar values. Trees, by contrast, can produce very different splits and/or predictions when the training data are perturbed. 

Why use very deep trees? The mechanics of bagging are designed to increase the diversity of the predicted values produced by each tree. Using a bootstrap sample, some training set samples are removed entirely, while others are replicated multiple times. This data perturbation encourages different trees. Using _unpruned_ and maximally grown trees is another technique to diversify predictions. We know very large trees are more likely to overfit by overreacting to specific training set points. This is generally bad. However, in ensembles, we _want_ higher variance from diverse predictions. 

```{r}
#| label: cls-bagging-demo
#| include: false
#| cache: true

extr_term_nodes <- function(x) {
  require(tidymodels)
  require(lorax)
  bag_obj <- 
    x |> 
    extract_fit_engine() 
  
  num_nodes <- 
    bag_obj$model_df$model |> 
    purrr::map_int(
      ~ .x |> extract_fit_engine() |> lorax::extract_rules() |> nrow()) |> 
    sum()
  
  tibble::tibble(num_terminal_nodes = num_nodes)
}

bag_wflow <-
  workflow(
    class ~ .,
    bag_tree(
      min_n = tune(),
      cost_complexity = tune(),
      mode = "classification"
    ) |>
      set_engine("rpart", time = 50)
  )

bag_param <- 
  bag_wflow |> 
  extract_parameter_set_dials() |> 
  update(min_n = min_n(c(1, 100)))


set.seed(8262)
bag_res <-
  bag_wflow |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = forested_rs,
    grid = 25,
    param_info = bag_param,
    control = control_grid(extract = extr_term_nodes)
  )
```

To demonstrate, we used the forestation data and created bagged CART ensembles with a range of tuning parameter values to see how tree complexity affects performance. A variety of bagged trees with 50 members, $\alpha \in [10^{-10}, 10^{-1}]$ and $n_{min} \in [1, 100]$ were resampled^[Where $\alpha$ is the cost-complexity parameters from @eq-cost-complexity.]. The figure shows the results where complexity was measured using the average number of terminal nodes within the ensemble. Clearly, simple (i.e., shallow) trees make poor ensembles. As we increase model complexity, performance improves rapidly before plateauing at low Brier scores. This was not a tuning exercise; we generally don't tune these models. This analysis shows that, in ensembles, maximum complexity equates to prediction diversity, which drives predictive performance. CITE PERFORMANCE for main model versus individual trees

```{r}
#| label: fig-cls-bagging-complexity
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: "center"
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: The relationship between tree complexity and performance for a bagged ensemble of 50 CART trees.
#| warning: false
#| message: false

bag_res |> 
  collect_extracts() |> 
  select(.config, .extracts) |> 
  unnest(.extracts) |> 
  summarize(
    num_terminal_nodes = mean(num_terminal_nodes),
    .by = c(.config)
  ) |> 
  full_join(
    collect_metrics(bag_res, type = "wide"), 
    by = join_by(.config)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(num_terminal_nodes / 50, brier_class)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, span = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(y = "Brier Class", x = "Mean # Terminal Nodes per Tree") 
```

Do other models benefit from being combined in a bagged ensemble? Neural networks for small to medium training sets are fairly unstable. Perturbing the data _and the random seed_ can generate different models and predictions. $K$-nearest neighbors are also very unstable. However, training them with a bagged tree may not be a good idea since a bootstrapped training set contains 2 or more replicated training samples. For $K < 10$, it may not be difficult to produce neighbors that are themselves (resulting in zero error). MARS/FDA models are slightly unstable. In our experience, adaptive regression splines produce diversity in split points when the underlying trend is not linear. For example, if a predictor and the outcome have a quadratic relationship, bagging produces similar models with split points that cluster where the derivative is near zero (e.g., the inflection point). Bagging these models can slightly improve performance. 

Next we'll talk about a generalization of bagged trees: random forests. 

## Random Forest {#sec-cls-rand-forest}

```{r}
#| label: forest-rf-ranger
#| include: false
#| cache: true

  rand_forest(
    mode = "classification",
    mtry = tune(),
    trees = 1000
  )

set.seed(526)
forest_rngr_res <-
  rngr_spec |>
  tune_grid(

forest_rngr_mtr_ex <-
```


Canonically, this model is the same as a bagging ensemble, with one additional feature designed to make its constituent trees more diverse [@breiman2001random]. Recall that most decision trees are _greedy_ since they choose the best predictor and split point that has the best result at the current location in the tree. They focus on the choice that matters most at that specific point. 

Random forests include an integer tuning parameter commonly called $m_{try}$: at each split point in each tree, the model considers only a random subset of $m_{try}$  predictors as the split variable. This significantly influences the makeup of the trees since the best possible decision may not be possible. It is likely suboptimal and might very well be detrimental to the tree _at that stage_. However, from the ensemble's perspective, the trees are good enough to use and become less correlated with one another, promoting additional tree diversity. In the end, using $m_{try}$ usually improves the model's efficacy. 

@fig-forest-splits shows several individual trees for the forestation data. Each panel fits an artificially small tree on these data and controls the random seed between plots. The blocks in the terminal nodes visualize the relative proportions of the classes from the training set for each rule. Trees (a) and (b) are standard CART fits that are trained on two different bootstrap samples. We can see that the structure is the same, but the split _values_ are slightly different. Tree (c) uses the same bootstrap samples as (a) but uses $m_{try} = 3$ instead of all predictors. We can see a completely different tree structure, with mostly different variables from the previous two trees.

However, using $m_{try}$ has a few downsides. First, to ensure informative predictors have enough opportunities to be considered in the split, we have to drastically increase the number of trees in the ensemble. At a minimum, 500 trees are needed, but 1,000 to 2,000 trees are recommended to have a reliable model. The second downside is that it somewhat compromises random forests' ability to perform automatic feature selection. Many uninformative predictors will be selected for a split. Fortunately, random forests pioneered permutation importance, which we discuss in @sec-importance. The original reference for the model suggests using a default value of $m_{try} = \sqrt{p}$ for classification models, where $p$ is the number of predictors. 

For the forestation data, a random forest model was optimized over $m_{try}$ for all 16 possible values. Each ensemble consisted of 1,000 trees. The results are shown in @fig-forest-splits along with some variants of the model that will be discussed below. We can see that there is a noticeable trend in the data for this model that results in an optimal value of $m_{try} = `r forest_rngr_best$mtry[1]`$, the y-axis shows that the range of possible results is extremely narrow. Almost any of these values would be suitable. This is quite often the pattern that we see for this model.

This robustness to tuning parameters reflects how low-maintenance random forest models are overall. They require very little tuning, need no variable transformations, can leave categorical predictors as-is, and, depending on the implementation, can naturally handle missing data. On average, they rank in the top 10% of models (in terms of performance) and, although they probably aren't uniformly optimal, they can produce a high-quality model with little effort.  

As one would expect with such a popular model, there have been a multitude of other extensions and enhancements to the standard model. For example, there are also variations of this model for ordinal outcomes [@janitza2016random;@hornung2020ordinal]. Also, there are direct analogs to different single-tree methods described in the previous chapter. For example, instead of CART models, conditional inference trees [@hothorn2006unbiased] can be used as the ensemble's constituents. This offers some improvements, especially if you want to reduce bias in split selection. As will be described in a later chapter, random forests are a primary tool for measuring how important predictors are to the outcome. Random forest variable importance methods are not perfect, but using conditional inference trees makes them more accurate because the model is not predisposed to select predictors based on how many unique values they contain. For comparison, we also tuned this approach over $m_{try}$. The available implementation is limited to categorical predictors with less than 24 splits, so an effect encoding preprocesspor was used on the county predictor. 

@fig-forest-rf shows that, for these data, the conditional inference forest results are slightly worse than the CART ensemble but are most likely practically equivalenet. In this case, $m_{try} = `r forest_crf_best$mtry[1]`$ was found to be optimal. 

Additionally, you can use oblique trees [@menze2011oblique;@jaeger2019oblique]. In this case, $m_{try}$ controls how many randomly selected predictors should make up the linear projection used for each split. This functional form likely has much lower variance than rectangular splits, so using it in a random forest model may not be as much of an upgrade as it is for traditional splits. Again, @fig-forest-rf shows these results for the implementation by @jaeger2022aorsf.  While slightly better than conditional inference trees in this analysis, they are minutely worse than traditional forests.  

Latly, we should mention extremely randomized trees (a.k.a. "extratrees"). These make splits completely at random and with the original training set. Essentially, these are unsupervised split candidates: a randomly chosen predictor and a randomly chosen split point [@geurts2006extremely]. It considers  $m_{try}$ random candidate splits and chooses the best among them. This approach is much faster because it avoids an exhaustive search across predictors. @fig-forest-splits demonstrates the effect of this method in panel (d) where randomized splits were used in conjunction with $m_{try} = 16$ so that 16 candidate splits were evaluated for each node. The structure, predictors, and split values differ significantly from the previous trees.  

@fig-forest-rf also shows the results of this model, which slightly edges out the traditional model but found $m_{try} = p$ to be optimal (and is, in essence, bagging). 

## Bayesian Additive Regression Trees {#sec-cls-bart}

```{r}
#| label: forest-bart
#| include: false
#| cache: true

extract_bart <- function(x) {
  require(tidymodels)
  x <- extract_fit_engine(x)
  trees <- dbarts::extract(x, "trees")
  num_term_nodes <- 
    trees |> 
    dplyr::filter(var == -1) |> 
    dplyr::count(tree, sample) |> 
    dplyr::summarize(mean_num_term_node = mean(n)) |> 
    purrr::pluck(1)
  nms <- colnames(x$varcount)
  is_county <- grepl("county", nms)
  num_used <- apply(x$varcount[, !is_county], 2, function(x) any(x > 0))
  cat_used <- any(apply(x$varcount[, is_county], 2, function(x) any(x > 0)))
  vars_used <- sum(c(num_used, cat_used))
  tibble(num_term_nodes = num_term_nodes, num_vars_used = vars_used)
}

bart_spec <-
  parsnip::bart(
    mode = "classification",
    trees = 100,
    prior_terminal_node_coef = tune(),
    prior_terminal_node_expo = tune(),
    prior_outcome_range = tune()
  ) |>
  set_engine("dbarts", keepevery = 10, nskip = 5000L, keeptrees = TRUE)

bart_wflow <- workflow(class ~ ., bart_spec)

bart_param <- 
  bart_wflow |> 
  extract_parameter_set_dials() |> 
  update(
    prior_outcome_range = prior_outcome_range(c(0.5, 5)),
    prior_terminal_node_coef = prior_terminal_node_coef(c(0.1, 1))
  )

set.seed(637)
forest_bart_res <-
  bart_spec |>
  tune_grid(
    class ~ .,
    resamples = forested_rs,
    grid = 25,
    param_info = bart_param, 
    control = control_grid(
      save_pred = TRUE,
      save_workflow = TRUE,
      extract = extract_bart
    ),
    metrics = cls_mtr
  )

forest_bart_best <- select_best(forest_bart_res, metric = "brier_class")

forest_bart_pred <-
  forest_bart_res |>
  collect_predictions(parameters = forest_bart_best) |>
  mutate(wflow_id = "BART") |>
  relocate(wflow_id)

forest_bart_mtr_ex <-
  forest_bart_pred |>
  cls_mtr(class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes)
```

Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) model the outcome with a sum of many small trees [@bart2010;@chipman2006bayesian]. We place prior distributions on each tree's structure, on its leaf parameters, and on the amount of shrinkage. While the model is more complex, the general process mirrors the one described in @sec-logistic-bayes. 

To estimate the model, we use MCMC to sample from the model's posterior distribution. Each MCMC iteration updates every tree in turn and yields one complete ensemble. After the chains converge to the posterior, we can sample from it to create a set of trees that define the ensemble. 

To start, let's denote a specific tree as $\mathcal{T}$ (as in the previous chapter) and parameters associated with its terminal nodes as $\Theta$. These parameters are not the probability estimates; they are on the real line and are similar to linear predictor values. 

For a specific predictor vector $\boldsymbol{x}$, the function $g(\boldsymbol{x}, \mathcal{T}, \Theta)$ returns the element in $\Theta$ corresponding to the terminal node where $\boldsymbol{x}$ lands. 

The overall BART model averages these estimates across $T$ trees to produce:

$$
\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{T} g(\boldsymbol{x};\, \mathcal{T}_j, \Theta_j)
$$

which is also on the real line. As we'll see below, this value is converted to a probability scale for the final prediction. 

Since BART is a Bayesian method, it relies heavily on probability and likelihood functions for computations. We typically assume that a binary outcome follows a Bernoulli distribution. To make the computations more tractable, BART takes a different approach that focuses on Gaussian quantities [@albert1993bayesian]. It defines a latent Gaussian random variable

$$
Z_i = \mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) + \gamma + \varepsilon_i
$$

where $\gamma$ is a user-defined offset, and $\varepsilon_i$ is an error term assumed to follow a standard normal distribution. The offset defaults to $\gamma = 0$ but can be used to address class imbalance. For example, if the event rate were 10% in the data, we might set $\gamma = \Phi^{-1}(0.1) \approx -1.28$ to help the model perform effectively, where $\Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse of the cumulative normal distribution function $\Phi$. The ensemble starts with $T$ trees with no splits, so $\hat{\mathcal{F}} = 0$. 

After the model is finalized, our probability estimates are then

$$
Pr\big[Y_i|\boldsymbol{x}_i\big] = \Phi\Big(\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(x_i) + \gamma\Big)
$$ {#eq-bart-prob}

There are two main sets of priors. The first is the tree-structure prior, which describes the probability that a specific node $\mathcal{N}$ in the tree should be split. This prior is parameterized as:

$$
Pr[{\text{split}}\;\mathcal{N}] = \alpha\,(1 + d_{\mathcal{N}})^{-\beta}
$$ {#eq-bart-depth-prior}

where $d_{\mathcal{N}}$ is the current depth of the prior and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ default to 0.95 and 2.0, respectively. @fig-tree-prior shows how the two parameters relate to the probability. @fig-tree-prior demonstrates how this equation captures our belief about the model. If we think we will need a set of deeper trees to predict the outcome accurately, smaller exponents with a larger coefficient are a good option. Exponents greater than 2.0 are the right choice if we believe a collection of small trees (perhaps even a single split) is best. If we have no _a priori_ thoughts on the matter, we can tune these parameters to see whether larger or smaller trees fit our data better. This parameterization helps us define what is plausible before seeing the data.


::: {#fig-tree-prior}

::::: {.figure-content}

```{r}
#| label: tree-prior
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3

depth_prior <- function(depth, alpha = 0.95, beta = 2.0) {
  dplyr::tibble(depth = depth, alpha = alpha, beta = beta) |> 
    dplyr::mutate(
      probability = alpha * (1 + depth)^(-beta)
    )
}

combos <- crossing(alpha = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.9), beta = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5))

dpth <- 1:10


prior_probs <- NULL
for (i in 1:nrow(combos)) {
  prior_probs <- 
    bind_rows(prior_probs,
              depth_prior(dpth, alpha = combos$alpha[i], beta = combos$beta[i]))
}

prior_probs |>
  mutate(alpha = format(alpha), Exponenet = beta) |>
  ggplot(aes(depth, probability, col = alpha, pch = alpha)) +
  geom_point(cex = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 1 / 2) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Exponenet, labeller = label_both, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(
    x = "Tree Depth",
    y = "Probability",
    col = "Coefficient",
    pch = "Coefficient"
  )
```

:::::

The effect of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ parameters for the prior associated with tree depth. 

:::

There are also uniform priors to select the predictor and the split point (based on a quantile or percent of the predictor's range). 

What about the terminal node parameters? The individual values are assumed to be Gaussian $\theta_i \sim N\big(0, \sigma_\theta^2\big)$. The corresponding variance is 
$$
\sigma_\theta = \frac{\kappa}{k\sqrt{T}}. 
$$

$\kappa$ is a scaling factor that specifies the usable probit range to effectively be $\pm \kappa$. Its default is 3.0. The parameter $k$ helps modulate how many prior standard deviations $\mathcal{F}$ stays inside that range define by $\kappa$. $k$ can shrink or expand the prior variance in the denominator, allowing more (or fewer) extreme probabilities to be plausible. 

The MCMC process for BART is somewhat more complex than the algorithm previously demonstrated for logistic regression. If we run the MCMC chain for $B$ iterations, we will actually make $B\times T$ accept/reject decisions. Each tree in the ensemble goes through the process, rather than one proposal for the whole ensemble. For each tree, these steps are executed: 

1. Remove tree $j$ from the ensemble and calculate its partial residual. These are the current estimate of the latent variable $Z$.
2. Propose a new tree structure
3. Sample from the leaf prior. 
4. Compute the likelihood with the new values. 
5. Accept/reject this tree

For the first step, we can rewrite the latent model as

$$
Z_i - \gamma = \sum_{j=1}^{T} g(\boldsymbol{x}_i; \mathcal{T}_j, \Theta_j) + \varepsilon_i
$$

The partial residual fixes the predictions for the other trees and subtracts them from the current estimate of the latent variable and its offset: 

$$
R_{ij} = (Z_i - \gamma) - \sum_{l \neq j} g(\boldsymbol{x}_i; \mathcal{T}_l, \Theta_l)
$$

Since we treat the other trees' predictions as constants, we can assume the partial residuals are also Gaussian. The partial residuals are now the response variable in a one-tree Gaussian regression^[We'll see that the sequential use of partial residuals is the backbone of the boosting methods described in the next section. BART's use of them _is not_ the same; it is not boosting. The residuals are used in a cyclic, round-robin way. Boosting uses them differently.]. These values are used to compute the current likelihood. 

For the second step, proposals for new trees use the operations described in @sec-cls-tree-global to grow, prune, and mutate trees (specifically @fig-tree-mutation). See @chipman1998bayesian. One implementation [@dbarts] uses: 

- Pr[split a leaf into two children] = 0.25
- Pr[collapse two sibling leaves into their parent] = 0.25
- Pr[redraw the cutpoint of an internal node's rule] = 0.40
- Pr[exchange the rules of a parent and child internal node] = 0.10

The steps 3 and 5 in the MCMC process for individual trees are more conventional. However, the likelihood is complex, so we'll skip the mechanics of how it is computed, but note that our Gaussian assumptions make the likelihood and posterior analytically tractable and efficient to compute. These models employ an impressive number of computational tricks. For example, we never evaluate the likelihood over the full data. Instead, we retain various sufficient statistics at the leaf level, which makes the Metropolis-Hastings computations very efficient. See @kapelner2013bartmachine, @pratola2014parallel, @emh, and @he2019xbart for more details. 

We sample the priors for hundreds (or thousands) of iterations. If we believe that the process has converged, we generate our final set of $T$ trees for the ensemble. 

To demonstrate, a BART model was tuned over $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from @eq-bart-prob as well as the $k$ value in $\sigma_\theta$. The model specification used $T$ = 100, required 1,0000 warm-up iterations, and retained every 10 pulls from the posterior distribution. The implementation required converting the categorical predictor to indicator variables before model training. @fig-forest-bart shows how the tuning parameters relate to the Brier score. A panel also shows the average number of terminal nodes produced within each tree. The $\alpha$ parameter performed better when close to its upper range, consistent with the parameter's default value ($\alpha$). The exponent ($\beta$) showed little signal for these data. The $k$ multiplier parameter showed a strong effect, with larger values being worse. The final panel shows that more terminal nodes were better (as a consequence of the depth parameters). 

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-bart
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "Tuning results for BART. The panel on the right reflects the average number of terminal nodes in the ensemble for different tuning parameter candidates."

bart_ord <- 
  c("Depth Prior Coefficient", "Depth Prior Exponent", 
    "Range Multiplier", "# Terminal Nodes")

forest_bart_res |>
  collect_extracts() |>
  unnest(.extracts) |>
  summarize(
    num_term_nodes = mean(num_term_nodes),
    .by = c(.config)
  ) |>
  full_join(
    forest_bart_res |>
      collect_metrics(type = "wide"),
    by = ".config"
  ) |>
  rename(
    `# Terminal Nodes` = num_term_nodes,
    `Depth Prior Coefficient` = prior_terminal_node_coef,
    `Depth Prior Exponent` = prior_terminal_node_expo,
    `Range Multiplier` = prior_outcome_range
  ) |> 
  select(-mn_log_loss, -roc_auc, -pr_auc) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    -c(.config, brier_class),
    names_to = "parameter",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(parameter = factor(parameter, levels = bart_ord)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, brier_class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 2 / 4, cex = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  labs(y = "Brier Score", x = NULL)
```

In the end, the chosen parameter candidates were $\alpha$ = `r round(forest_bart_best$prior_terminal_node_coef, 2)`, $\beta$ = `r round(forest_bart_best$prior_terminal_node_expo, 2)`, and $k = `r round(forest_bart_best$prior_outcome_range, 2)`$ with a corresponding Brier score was `r round(forest_bart_mtr_ex$.estimate[forest_bart_mtr_ex$.metric == "brier_class"], 3)`.

## Boosting {#sec-cls-boosting}

Boosted trees are ensembles of decision trees created sequentially, with each new member reacting to what occurred in the previous tree(s). The tree ensembles discussed so far create a collection of independent trees. Boosting, by contrast, is an iterative process. 

The boosting model that we think of today is an evolution of an idea that started in the 1980's. @valiant1984 described machine learning models within a theoretical framework for "weak" and "strong" learners, depending on whether they could reach an arbitrarily small error rate. A weak learner was considered barely better than random guessing. @kearns1988 posed the question, "Can we convert a weak learner to a strong one?" and coined the term "boosting." @schapire1990 showed the equivalence of strong and weak learnability and outlined a general algorithm in which a sequence of (binary) classifiers can compensate for the shortcomings of previous models. @freund1995 produced a more specific framework where the collection of models predicted via a majority vote rule, and drucker1993 showed an application of boosting with neural networks. 

The first landmark boosting algorithm was the AdaBoost model of @freundschapire1997. This model used a case-weighting system that helped each learner emphasize training-set points poorly predicted by previous models (i.e., difficult points received larger weights for the next model). Each tree in the ensemble had a corresponding stage weight based on its current error rate. The final prediction was a weighted average of each model's predictions, using the stage weight as the weight. It also used an exponential loss function. At this point, the algorithm was constrained to binary classification and produced only hard-class predictions. In @freundschapire1996, they used C4.5 classifiers as the weak learner. 

This is also when Breiman defined the previously described bagging model, and a flurry of papers investigated how AdaBoost worked. It is also when @breiman1999 and @mason2000 realized that the boosting algorithm was conducting _gradient descent_. It is also when the landmark paper @friedman2000 showed the same, noted that the model was an additive function of individual models, and that AdaBoost's current exponential loss function was similar to (but not equivalent to) the binomial log-likelihood. Their initial model, LogistBoost, gave a more familiar theoretical statistical framework and generalized the model to include some tuning parameters. 

Arguably, the first lasting definition of gradient boosting quickly followed in @friedman2001. It solidified boosting as a gradient descent algorithm and 

- Generalized the objective function to be any log-likelihood.
- Showed that the gradient function was represented as pseudo-residuals (recall the residuals from @sec-tree-splitting).
- Introduced a learning rate parameter.

This extended boosting to regression models, multi-class classification, and other models. It also framed the learning rate as a form of regularization. The author also introduced relative-importance measures and partial dependence plots for model interpretability.

The next leap forward was @friedman2002. Perhaps influenced by SGD, Friedman defined stochastic gradient boosting (SGB). At each stage, the model is fit on a random subset of the training set. This decorrelates the trees and improves their effectiveness. It also trains faster.

While some small improvements have been made, fundamentally, most modern boosting models are implementations of stochastic gradient boosting. The current slate of top-performing models (XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) are based on this model and are mostly focused on the engineering aspects of the computations. 


```{r}
#| label: forest-boost-c5

#| cache: true

  boost_tree(
    mode = "classification",
    trees = tune(),
    min_n = tune()

  set_engine("C5.0")

set.seed(498)
forest_c5_res <-
  c5_spec |>
  tune_grid(
    class ~ .,
    resamples = forested_rs,
    grid = 25,
    control = control_grid(
      save_pred = TRUE,
      save_workflow = TRUE

    metrics = cls_mtr
  )

forest_c5_best <- select_best(forest_c5_res, metric = "brier_class")

forest_c5_pred <-
  forest_c5_res |>
  collect_predictions(parameters = forest_c5_best) |>
  mutate(wflow_id = "Boosted C5.0") |>
  relocate(wflow_id)

forest_c5_mtr_ex <-
  forest_c5_pred |>
  cls_mtr(class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes)
```

Modern boosting methods do not use sample reweighting to create ensemble members. Although AdaBoost has not persisted as a commonly used method, one sample-weighting method has. C5.0 is a modern successor to Quinlan's C4.5 model. Let's discuss this method for diving into other techniques. 

### Classical Boosting {#sec-cls-classic-boosting}

C5.0 has several minor differences from its predecessor and also enables boosting via reweighting. Like modern methods, this boosting tool includes a significant amount of engineering embedded within. For example, C5.0 conducts a kind of futility analysis to determine whether training-set points it will _never_ be able to predict correctly and drops them. This discussion provides a general overview of what the methodology does and how well it works. 

So far, we have not discussed **case weights**. These values, associated with each training set sample, often measure how much influence a specific data point should have on computations such as the model's objective function. A wide variety of case weights can be used in different phases (e.g., training, model assessment, etc.). For example, frequency weights are integer values that indicate how often a specific data vector occurs. For example, if the forestation included only the county predictor, we could reduce the training set to `r length(levels(forested_train$county))` rows (one per county) and assign a corresponding frequency weight based on how often each county occurs.  

Our focus here is on importance weights, which are general non-negative values used during model training. Most of our models can already accommodate case weights during computations. We define the training set case weights as $w_i$ ($i=1\ldots n_{tr}$), initialized to 1.0 (unless the user overrides this default), and fit the first tree in the ensemble with each training set sample having the same influence on the model.  After this fit, the number of leaves in this tree is used to limit the dpeth of future trees to make all trees about the same size. 
 
After training tree $\mathcal{T}_j$ of $T$ in the ensemble, the current tree classifies the entire training set. This is also when C5.0 conducts its futility analysis to determine which (if any) points to exclude. We'll denote the available training set points at iteration $j$ as $n_{(j)}$. 

The probability estimate for class $k$ for tree $j$ is the class-specific count in the node divided by the total count. With missing data, the estimate is a weighted average of the terminal nodes into which its fractional weight was distributed. This is the estimate used (internally) during training and, when predicting new samples, the corrected values described in @sec-tree-estimates are the estimates. 

The case-weight update algorithm depends on whether the model predicted samples correctly or incorrectly. When the model predicts the correct class, the weights are scaled _multiplicatively_, while the poorly predicted ones have an _additive_ increase.  For tree $j$, we denote the total weights for correctly and incorrectly predicted samples as $W_{+}^{(j)}$ and $W_{-}^{(j)}$, respectively. Also, $\mathcal{E}^{(j)}$ is the unweighted number of misclassified active samples. From these, we compute:

$$
\begin{align}
\delta^{(j)} &= \frac{W_{+}^{(j)} - W_{-}^{(j)}}{4} \notag \\
a^{(j)} &= \frac{W_{+}^{(j)} - \delta^{(j)}}{W_{+}^{(j)}} \notag \\
b^{(j)} &= \frac{\delta^{(j)}}{\mathcal{E}^{(j)}} \notag \\
\nu^{(j)} &= \frac{n_{(j)}}{W_{+}^{(j)} + W_{-}^{(j)}} \notag 
\end{align}
$$

$\delta^{(j)}$ is _how much_ weight moves. This is the total weight taken from the correctly classified group and given to the misclassified group. It is set so that the misclassified group's total ends up halfway between its current total, $W_{-}^{(j)}$, and half of all the weight.  

The case-weight update is then: 

$$
w_i^{(j+1)} =
\begin{cases}
\max\left(\nu^{(j)}\, a^{(j)}\, w_i^{(j)},\ 0.001\right) & \text{if correctly predicted}  \\
\nu^{(j)}\left(w_i^{(j)} + b^{(j)}\right) & \text{if incorrectly predicted} \\
0 & \text{if dropped}
\end{cases}
$$

$a^{(j)}$ represents how much each correctly classified sample shrinks and $b^{(j)}$ is the additional weight that incorrect samples recieve. The factor $\nu^{(j)}$ makes the active weights sum to $n_{(j)}$.


To make the final ensemble prediction, C5.0 uses the sum of the weights for class $k$ in terminal node $\ell$ for tree $j$ ($n_{\ell k}^{(j)}$) as well as the total weights over classes ($n_{\ell}^{(j)}$). They also use the observer class prevalences from the training set ($p_k$). The hard class prediction is determined by finding the largest value for the node that the new sample lands in (denoted as $\ell$ here): 

$$
\widehat{y}^{(j)} = \arg\max_k n_{\ell k}^{(j)}
$$

The shrunken terminal node proportion is computed (as mentioned in the previous chapter)

$$
\widetilde{p}_k^{(j)} = \frac{n_{\ell k}^{(j)} + p_k^{(j)}}{n_{\ell}^{(j)} + 1}
$$

where $p_k^{(j)}$ is the proportion determined from the data currently in each tree^[Since some training set samples may have been abandoned.]. For the tree, the _confidence value_ is the shrunken proportion corresponding to the predicted class $\widehat{y}^{(j)}$. We'll call that $\widetilde{p}^{(j)}$. 

Now that we have estimated confidence values for each tree, the final estimate for an unknown sample is a weighted average of the votes: 

$$
\widehat{p}_{k} = \frac{\sum\limits_{j=1}^{T} \widetilde{p}^{(j)}\, I\big[\widehat{y}^{(j)} = k\big]}{\sum \limits_{j=1}^{T^{}} \widetilde{p}^{(j)}}
$$

The binary class votes provides more weight to trees that have the largest confidence values. 



### Modern Boosting {#sec-cls-modern-boosting}

As with the BART discussion, we'll denote a linear predictor type quantity as $\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$, which is on the real line. For trees, this is not a linear combination of parameters, but a set of conditional logic statements that yield a single numeric score. This score can be converted to a probability-like format via the logistic function

$$
p(\boldsymbol{x}_i)= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)}}
$$

A boosted tree ensemble is a sum of $T$ trees:

$$
\mathcal{F}_T = \mathcal{F}_0 + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{T} \mathcal{T}_j
$$

where $\alpha$ is the learning rate and $\mathcal{F}_0$ is an initial score value. 

As we mentioned earlier, most commonly used gradient boosting models use the log-likelihood [@sec-cross-entropy] as the objective function (previously denoted as $\psi()$ in @sec-gradient-opt). For simplicity, we'll focus on $C=2$ classes. As a reminder, for the Bernoulli distribution, that function is

$$
\ell(y_i, \mathcal{F}_i) = -\Big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i) \Big]
$$

using $\mathcal{F}_i$ as shorthand for $\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$. Written in terms of the score, this simplifies to:

$$
\ell(y_i, \mathcal{F}_i) = \log\left(1 + e^{\mathcal{F}_i}\right) - y_i \mathcal{F}_i
$$

It is common to add a penalty to this loss function: 

The full objective adds a penalty $\mathcal{P}$ on the complexity of each tree:

$$
\psi() = \sum_{i=1}^{n_{tr}} \ell(y_i, \mathcal{F}_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{T} \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{T}_j)
$$

for some penalty function $\mathcal{P}$. Now that we have the objective function, what are the gradient and Hessian?

First, the deverivatives are with respect to the $\mathcal{F}_i$ so there are $n_{tr}$ elements. We'll eventually want to parameterize the gradient as a function of $p_i$ instead of $\mathcal{F}_i$. For that, we need:

$$
\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial \mathcal{F}_i} = \frac{e^{-\mathcal{F}_i}}{\left(1 + e^{-\mathcal{F}_i}\right)^2} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathcal{F}_i}}}_{p_i} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{e^{-\mathcal{F}_i}}{1 + e^{-\mathcal{F}_i}}}_{1 - p_i} = p_i (1 - p_i)
$$

We'll also need

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial p_i} = -\frac{y_i}{p_i} + \frac{1 - y_i}{1 - p_i} = \frac{-y_i (1 - p_i) + (1 - y_i) p_i}{p_i (1 - p_i)} = \frac{p_i - y_i}{p_i (1 - p_i)}
$$

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
g_i = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathcal{F}_i} = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial p_i} \cdot \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial \mathcal{F}_i} = \frac{p_i - y_i}{p_i (1 - p_i)} \cdot p_i (1 - p_i) = p_i - y_i
$$
 
This is the raw residual $e_{ik}$ from @sec-tree-splitting which ranges from $[-1, 1]$. 

The Hessian is much more straightforward: 

$$
h_i = \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \mathcal{F}_i^2} = p_i (1 - p_i)
$$

This matches the variance of the Bernoulli distribution, is non-negative, and is maximized at $1/C = 0.5$. Recall that the Hessian is a _matrix_ with partial derivatives on the off-diagonals. Gradient boosting uses the approximation all $h_{ii'} = 0$ for all $i \ne i'$. 

We'll denote $G$ and $H$ as the sum of the $g_i$ and $h_i$ over the training set.

```{r}
load("../RData/forest_c5_set_res.RData")
load("../RData/forest_cit_set_res.RData")
load("../RData/forested_obl_set_res.RData")
load("../RData/forest_c5rules_set_res.RData")


forest_ensemble_set_res <-
  as_workflow_set(
    Bagged_CART = forest_cart_bag_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    RF = forest_rngr_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    `RF (ERT)` = forest_ert_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    `Oblique RF` = forest_rf_obl_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    Boost_C5.0 = forest_c5_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    XGBoost = forest_xgb_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    LightGBM = forest_lgb_res |> butcher::butcher(),
    BART = forest_bart_res |> butcher::butcher()
  )

all_sets <-
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    forest_fda_set_res,
    forest_knn_set_res,
    forest_glmnet_set_res,
    forest_logistic_set_res,
    forest_mlp_set_res,
    forest_tabpfn_set_res,
    forest_tabicl_set_res,
    forest_autoint_set_res,
    forest_saint_set_res,
    forested_obl_set_res,
    forest_cart_set_res,
    forest_c5_set_res,
    forest_c5rules_set_res,
    forest_cit_set_res,
    forest_crf_set_res, 
    forest_ensemble_set_res,
    forest_ctb_set_res
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: cls-ensemble-compare-bayes
#| include: false
#| cache: false
set.seed(905)
ensemble_compare <- compare_models(
  all_sets,
  chains = 10,
  cores = 10,
  iter = 5000
)

ensemble_best <- ensemble_compare$model[is.na(ensemble_compare$probability)]

ensemble_subset <-
  ensemble_compare |>
  mutate(
    # To get results for traditional and randomized RF 
    engine = if_else(grepl("ERT", model), "extratrees", engine)
  ) |> 
  slice_min(median, by = c(class, engine)) |>
  mutate(
    model = as.character(model),
    model = ifelse(grepl("basic_", model), "Oblique Tree", model),
    model = ifelse(
      grepl("logistic_mle", model),
      "Logistic (unpenalized)",
      model
    ),
    model = ifelse(grepl("1L", model), "MLP (1 Layer)", model),
    model = ifelse(grepl("2L", model), "MLP (2 Layers)", model),
    model = gsub("glmnet", "Logistic (penalized)", model),
    model = ifelse(grepl("basic_", model), "Oblique Tree", model),
    model = ifelse(grepl("tab_pfn", model), "TabPFN", model),
    model = ifelse(grepl("autoint", model), "AutoInt", model),
    model = gsub("_", " ", model),
    model = factor(model),
    model = reorder(model, median)
  )

ensemble_best_brier <- round(
  ensemble_subset$median[ensemble_subset$model == ensemble_best],
  3
)
```

How well do these models perform relative to previously discussed techniques?  @fig-cls-ensemble-compare visualizes the Brier score results across models. The Bayesian methods in @sec-compare-resample-bayes were used to estimate the probability distributions for each of the best candidates for each model. The intervals show the 0.05, 0.50, and 0.95 quantiles. Currently, the `r ensemble_best` model has the smallest Brier score with a Bayesian point estimate of `r ensemble_best_brier`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cls-ensemble-compare
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| out-width: 70%
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Comparisons of current forestation models. The intervals are 90% credible intervals. The bars on the right show the probability of practical equivalence to the current best model, assuming that a difference in Brier scores of +/- 0.01 is practical."
#| fig-alt: "Two-panel figure comparing all forestation models discussed so far. The left panel is a dot-and-whisker plot of Brier scores with 90% credible intervals, ordered from best to worst. Tree-based models cluster at higher Brier scores than the leading models. The right panel shows horizontal bars for the probability of practical equivalence, indicating that single tree models have virtually no chance of matching the currently best-performing models."
p_brier <-
  ensemble_subset |>
  ggplot(aes(median, model)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 1 / 2) +
  labs(y = NULL, x = "Brier Score") +
  theme(
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 2, b = 10, l = 10, unit = "pt")
  )

p_brier_diff <-
  ensemble_subset |>
  ggplot(aes(pract_equiv, model)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", aes(fill = pract_equiv), show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(y = NULL, x = "Pr[Equiv]") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = round((0:2) / 2, 2), limits = 0:1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 2, unit = "pt")
  )

p_brier + p_brier_diff + plot_layout(widths = c(4, 1))
```
